headline_en: Parliament special committee agrees on immunity for July uprising participants
summary_en: A special committee of Bangladesh's 13th parliament began reviewing 133 ordinances issued under the interim government, discussing about 40 at its first meeting on 24 March 2026. The list discussed included the human trafficking and migrant smuggling ordinance, the Overseas Employment and Migrants (Amendment) Ordinance and the Bangladesh Travel Agency (Registration and Control) (Amendment) Ordinance; decisions were not reached on all of them. The committee must report to parliament by 2 April.

facts.statement: On 24 March 2026 the Bangladesh parliament's special committee reviewing 133 ordinances issued by the interim government discussed about 40 ordinances at its first meeting, including one ordinance of the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment; not all received a decision.
facts.source_in_article: meeting sources; committee chair Joynul Abedin

facts.statement: Among the interim-government ordinances discussed by the parliament special committee on 24 March 2026 were the 'Manob Pachar o Obhibashi Chorachalan Protirodh o Domon Odhyadesh' (Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking and Migrant Smuggling Ordinance), the 'Boideshik Kormosongsthan o Obhibashi (Songshodhon) Odhyadesh' (Overseas Employment and Migrants (Amendment) Ordinance) and the Bangladesh Travel Agency (Registration and Control) (Amendment) Ordinance. The article does not say what was decided on these.
The parliament special committee was asked to report on the 133 interim-government ordinances to parliament by 2 April 2026; ordinances must be approved by parliament.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo; committee chair Joynul Abedin

186 of the Bangladeshis stranded in Iran on their way to Dhaka
summary_en: The first group of Bangladeshis stranded by the Iran war, 186 people, left Baku, Azerbaijan, for Dhaka on a special Biman Bangladesh flight on Friday 20 March 2026. A government delegation led by the ambassador to Turkey received them at Azerbaijan's Astara border and took them by bus to Baku airport. IOM helped move them from Tehran and other places in Iran to Baku.

facts.statement: On Friday 20 March 2026 at about 6:30 pm local time (8:30 pm Bangladesh time) a special Biman Bangladesh flight left Heydar Aliyev International Airport in Baku, Azerbaijan, for Dhaka carrying 186 Bangladeshis who had been stranded in Iran by the war: 11 women, 10 children and 165 men. This was the first group.
facts.source_in_article: Mohammad Shahnoor Ali, deputy chief of mission at the Bangladesh embassy in Turkey, who accompanied the group

facts.statement: The Bangladesh government sent a delegation led by its ambassador to Turkey, M Amanul Haque, to Azerbaijan on Wednesday (18 March 2026) to oversee the return of Bangladeshis from Iran; from the morning of Thursday 19 March it received the 186 Bangladeshis at Azerbaijan's Astara border and took them by bus to Baku airport.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM) helped bring the Bangladeshis from Tehran and other places in Iran to Baku airport for the March 2026 evacuation.

headline_en: BIMAS seeks Italian government solution on stay permits for Bangladeshis who came on sponsor visas
summary_en: At an iftar in Rome on 14 March 2026 organised by the Bangladesh Immigrants Association (BIMAS), its founding president Muktar Hossain told Italian politicians that many Bangladeshis who came to Italy on sponsor (flussi) visas from 2022 to date still have not received stay permits despite holding regular visas. The Bangladesh ambassador said over 2.5 lakh Bangladeshis live in Italy and praised BIMAS's Italian-language teaching. BIMAS said it would raise the issue after Ramadan.

facts.statement: Many Bangladeshis who came to Italy on sponsor (flussi, printed 'ফ্লস্সি') visas from 2022 up to March 2026 have still not received legal papers; despite holding regular visas and a 'nulla osta' (printed 'নুলা সস্তা'), they have not got a stay permit (permesso di soggiorno).
facts.source_in_article: Muktar Hossain, founding president of Bangladesh Immigrants Association (BIMAS), speaking at an iftar in Rome on 14 March 2026

facts.statement: BIMAS said it is looking for a solution on the stay-permit problem for flussi/sponsor-visa Bangladeshis and planned to discuss it with Italian politicians after Ramadan 2026, asking them to help.
More than about 2.5 lakh (250,000) Bangladeshis live in Italy, according to the Bangladesh ambassador in March 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh ambassador to Italy ATM Rokibul Haque

facts.statement: The Bangladesh ambassador to Italy said in March 2026 that Bangladeshis rank 6th among immigrants in Italy, but third within the Muslim community and first among Asians and South Asians; he also said 30 percent of 'about 90 percent of immigrants' in Italy are Muslim (wording as printed).
BIMAS (Bangladesh Immigrants Association) is a migrant association in Italy working on migrants' issues and runs Italian language teaching for the Bangla community, which the ambassador praised.

headline_en: 200 Bangladeshis returning from Iran before Eid
summary_en: With US and Israeli strikes on Iran continuing, the Bangladesh government decided to bring home several hundred Bangladeshis from Iran, about 200 in the first phase by road to Azerbaijan and then by Biman charter from Baku. A list of about 300 people was prepared for two phases. Azerbaijan approved on-arrival visas for 274 Bangladeshis and the embassy in Tehran gave travel passes to those without passports.

facts.statement: In March 2026 the Bangladesh government decided to bring back Bangladeshis in Iran who want to return, taking them by road to Azerbaijan (the ambassador said via the 'Iraq border', as printed) and then to Dhaka on a Biman Bangladesh chartered flight from Baku; about 200 were to come in the first phase within a few days.
facts.source_in_article: Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman; Ambassador to Turkey M Amanul Haque

facts.statement: A policy decision to bring Bangladeshis out of Iran was taken from the second week of March 2026; a list of about 300 people was made for return in two phases. Embassy diplomats, staff and their families were not in the first group of about 200.

Because Iran's embassy in Azerbaijan stopped operating in early March 2026, the Bangladesh embassy in Turkey coordinated with Azerbaijan's foreign ministry, and the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi worked with Azerbaijan's embassy in Delhi on visas.
facts.source_in_article: Diplomatic sources in Dhaka and Tehran

facts.statement: Bangladesh requested on-arrival visas from Azerbaijan's embassy in Delhi for 202 and then 72 people; Azerbaijan approved on-arrival visas for all 274 Bangladeshis leaving Iran in March 2026.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi sources

facts.statement: Not all Bangladeshis being returned from Iran in March 2026 had passports; those without passports were given travel passes by the Bangladesh embassy in Tehran.

headline_en: Special flight planned to bring home Bangladeshis stranded in Qatar
summary_en: Amid tension in the Gulf, the Bangladesh embassy in Doha said in an 11 March 2026 emergency notice that it is arranging a special flight with the Qatari government and Qatar Airways for stranded Bangladeshis. Families, women, children and the elderly get priority, and those wanting to return must register through a Google Form posted on the embassy's official social media.

facts.statement: In an emergency notice of 11 March 2026 the Bangladesh embassy in Doha said it was arranging a special flight home for Bangladeshis stranded in Qatar, working closely with the Qatari government and Qatar Airways.

To get on the embassy's special flight from Qatar (March 2026), stranded Bangladeshis must submit their details as soon as possible through a Google Form whose link is posted on the Bangladesh embassy in Doha's official social media platforms.
Families, women, children and elderly people wanting to return to Bangladesh get priority on the Doha embassy's special flight (March 2026).
Qatar is one of the main destinations for Bangladeshi workers, with large numbers working in construction, services and other sectors.

headline_en: Injured expatriate's last wish before death: to be buried in Makkah
summary_en: Mofizur Rahman (65) of Patiya, Chattogram, who had lived and worked in Makkah for 12 years, was hit by a car on the night of Monday 9 March 2026 while walking home after Tarawih prayers and died in hospital at about 1 am after Tuesday night. His kafil (employer) confirmed the death, and he is being buried in Makkah at his own request made to the kafil. He was his family's only earner and last visited home in 2009.

facts.statement: Mofizur Rahman (65), of Majherghata, ward 4, Patiya municipality, Chattogram, was hit by a vehicle in Makkah on Monday night (9 March 2026) while returning home after Tarawih prayers, was taken to a local hospital by people with him and died there at about 1 am in the night after Tuesday (10 March 2026).
When Mofizur Rahman died in Makkah in March 2026, a Saudi-based Bangladeshi called the family from his own mobile phone with the news, and his kafil (employer) confirmed the death.

Mofizur Rahman, dying in a Makkah hospital in March 2026, asked his kafil (employer) to have him buried in Makkah, and he is to be buried there; the family will therefore not see his face a last time.

headline_en: Food prices rising with oil in world markets; what will Bangladesh do
summary_en: An analysis of how the Israel-Iran war and the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz are pushing up oil and food prices. Among risks to Bangladesh it lists remittances: if Middle East economic activity slows, Bangladeshi workers there will be hurt, remittance inflows may fall and fewer new workers may go to the Middle East. Iran attacked a data centre in Qatar, and attacks hit sites in Bahrain, Qatar, Dubai and Kuwait.

facts.statement: Prothom Alo's analysis (March 2026) says remittance is a major risk from the Israel-Iran war: if economic activity in the Middle East slows, Bangladeshi workers there will be hurt, remittance flows to Bangladesh may fall, and the number of new workers going to the Middle East may fall.
Iran attacked a data centre in Qatar, which had a big effect on financial activity in the Middle East (March 2026).

According to the BBC, as cited by Prothom Alo in March 2026, there were repeated attacks on Bahrain's oil facilities, Qatar's gas processing centre, a port near Dubai's Palm island and oil tankers anchored off Kuwait.

headline_en: Bangladeshi exporters worried over Middle East conflict
summary_en: After US and Israeli forces attacked Iran on Saturday 28 February 2026, Iran struck US bases in several Middle Eastern countries including the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia and Iraq; air links in the region were temporarily shut and Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz. The article is mainly about export risks, but RAPID chairman MA Razzak warns that if Bangladeshis' workplaces in the Middle East are hit they will not be paid and remittances may fall.

facts.statement: After US and Israeli forces attacked Iran on Saturday morning (28 February 2026), Iran retaliated against Israel and US bases in Middle Eastern countries, including the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia and Iraq; all air travel in the region was temporarily stopped and Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz to all ships.

Many Bangladeshis work in the Middle East; if their workplaces are hit by the war they will not get wages, and remittances may fall, so the government must monitor carefully and be ready to act (March 2026).
facts.source_in_article: MA Razzak, chairman of research organisation RAPID

headline_en: Bangladesh-US relations: trade and geopolitics to feature in Paul Kapur's visit
summary_en: US Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asia Paul Kapur was to visit Dhaka 3 to 5 March 2026, the first senior US visit after Bangladesh's election. Washington sources said the return of Bangladeshis who are irregular in the US may be discussed: about 500 have been sent back so far and about 5,000 more are in the return process. Bangladesh planned to ask for B-1 visa relief to take businesspeople off the US visa bond list.

facts.statement: As of about 1 March 2026, about 500 Bangladeshis had been sent back from the United States, and about 5,000 more Bangladeshis who became irregular in the US were in the process of being returned; this was expected to be discussed during Paul Kapur's 3 to 5 March 2026 Dhaka visit.
Bangladesh planned to raise, during US Assistant Secretary Paul Kapur's March 2026 visit, a relaxation in the B-1 category so that Bangladeshi businesspeople are removed from the US visa bond list.

headline_en: Emergency message for Bangladeshi expatriates in six Middle East countries including Qatar, UAE, Kuwait
summary_en: On Saturday 28 February 2026, as war broke out in the Middle East, Bangladesh embassies in Lebanon, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq issued emergency advisories. Bangladeshis were told to stay away from military sites, stay in safe places, avoid going out and gatherings, obey local rules, keep documents and supplies at hand, and not post photos or videos or spread rumours, which is illegal in these countries. The article lists hotline numbers and emails for each mission.

facts.statement: On Saturday 28 February 2026 Bangladesh embassies in Lebanon, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq told Bangladeshis to stay away from military installations, stay in safe places until the danger passes, not go out unless essential, avoid gatherings and meetings, not spread rumours, and keep important papers and daily necessities close.
facts.source_in_article: Emergency notices of the Bangladesh embassies

facts.statement: The embassies' 28 February 2026 notices advised Bangladeshis in Lebanon, Qatar, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq to always keep with them cash, passport, local ID card, health card or health insurance, needed medicines, mobile charger, power bank, dry food and water, and to follow host-government instructions and respect local law.
facts.source_in_article: Emergency notices of the Bangladesh embassies

facts.statement: Some Bangladesh embassies warned in February 2026 that uploading photos or videos of the current (war) situation to social media and spreading baseless news is against the laws of these Middle Eastern countries, and told Bangladeshis not to do it.

The Bangladesh embassy in Lebanon told Bangladeshis living in the south and west (Bekaa Valley) and in southern Beirut (Dahiyeh) and nearby areas to move with special caution, not travel at night and avoid conflict areas (February 2026).

headline_en: Bangladeshi Tanim charms Qatar with his voice
summary_en: Tanim Hasan, a young hafiz from Pakundia, Kishoreganj, who came to Qatar in 2025 and has worked for eight months as a food-delivery bike rider, went viral after a Kenyan colleague posted his Quran recitation on TikTok on 20 February 2026. The CEO of delivery app company Snoonu sent him 5,000 Qatari riyals (over 1.5 lakh taka) and promised him an office job and an imam post, plus Umrah. He lives in the Sanaiya industrial area, Street 13.

facts.statement: Tanim Hasan, a Bangladeshi from Narandi union, Pakundia, Kishoreganj, came to Qatar in 2025 for a living and has worked for the past eight months as a bike rider for a food-delivery company; he lives in the Sanaiya industrial area, number 13.

After Tanim Hasan's Quran recitation video went viral in February 2026, Hamad Mubarak Al-Hajri, CEO of the delivery app company Snoonu (printed 'সুনুনো/সুনুনু'), sent him more than 1.5 lakh Bangladeshi taka (5,000 Qatari riyals) as a gift and promised a job at the company's office, an arrangement to serve as a mosque imam, and to take him on Umrah.
Prothom Alo's 'Dur Porobash' diaspora section takes stories, videos and photos from readers abroad at email dp@prothomalo.com.

headline_en: 'Save me, son... it hurts so much': no ICU could be found for him either
summary_en: Md Jahangir Alam (40) of Baliadanga, Satkhira, who went to Malaysia in 2018 through a broker at great expense, fell seriously ill there, was ruined by brokers in the name of treatment and returned on 17 February 2026. He died at Dhaka Medical College Hospital on 19 February without getting an ICU bed. His family mortgaged land and sold cattle to pay his treatment in Malaysia and in Dhaka. The article mainly covers the ICU shortage at DMCH.

facts.statement: Md Jahangir Alam (40) of Satkhira, who had gone to Malaysia in 2018, fell seriously ill there (acute necrotising pancreatitis, with no bowel movement for about a month and unable to eat), returned to Bangladesh on 17 February 2026, was taken round several Dhaka hospitals and admitted to Dhaka Medical College Hospital that night, and died there on the afternoon of 19 February 2026 without getting an ICU bed.
facts.source_in_article: DMC student Alfaz Hossain; son Afzal Hossain

facts.statement: Jahangir Alam went to Malaysia in 2018 through a broker (dalal) after spending a lot of money; the amount is not given.
In Malaysia, sick Bangladeshi worker Jahangir Alam was ruined by brokers in the name of treatment: he spent money but did not get proper treatment.

Jahangir Alam could not send money home regularly from Malaysia; his family mortgaged land and sold cattle to cover his treatment costs in Malaysia and his hospital costs after returning to Bangladesh in February 2026.

Dhaka Medical College Hospital has 2,600 beds but over 4,000 admitted patients, 140 ICU beds in 8 ICUs, and a waiting list of over 40 patients per ICU bed; a senior official says at least 400 ICU beds are needed. Private-hospital ICU costs are beyond low- and middle-income families (one Dhanmondi private hospital quoted 50,000-60,000 taka per day in a 2023 case).
facts.source_in_article: Unnamed senior DMCH official; Prothom Alo 2023 report

headline_en: Elder brother had to leave for Saudi Arabia leaving his younger brother's body behind
summary_en: On Monday 23 February 2026 at about 6 am, a microbus taking Mehedi Hasan (25) of Brahmanpara, Cumilla, to Dhaka airport for his 1:20 pm flight to Saudi Arabia hit a stopped truck at Malikhil, Daudkandi, on the Dhaka-Chattogram highway, killing his brother Ibrahim Khalil (14) and the driver-owner Md Shahin (40). Mehedi, himself injured, flew to Saudi Arabia without burying his brother because his visa had no time left, his uncle said.

facts.statement: At about 6 am on Monday 23 February 2026, a microbus carrying Saudi-bound worker Mehedi Hasan (25) and his family from Cumilla to Dhaka airport rear-ended a truck that stopped suddenly at Malikhil, Daudkandi upazila, on the Dhaka-Chattogram highway; his brother Ibrahim Khalil (14) and driver-owner Md Shahin (40) of Charipara died on the spot, and Mehedi was injured.
facts.source_in_article: Police and family; Daudkandi Highway Police SI Md Zakir Hossain

facts.statement: Mehedi Hasan's uncle said Mehedi's visa had no validity left ('ভিসার মেয়াদ ছিল না'), so he had no choice but to take his 1:20 pm flight to Saudi Arabia on 23 February 2026, leaving his brother's body unburied, for the sake of his livelihood.

headline_en: A mandate for measurable change and a new chapter of economic growth
summary_en: An opinion column by Dr Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir on BNP's election win and economic plans. It notes that expanding the international labour market is one of the core elements of BNP's job-creation plan, alongside technical education and skills, and that remittances play an important role in the economy.

headline_en: BG 387, my experience
summary_en: A reader's account of a Biman Bangladesh flight from Kuala Lumpur to Dhaka on 1 January (New Year's Day), full mostly of migrant workers going home on short leave, which was diverted to Yangon because fog closed Dhaka, Chattogram and Sylhet airports. Passengers were kept in the hot plane for about three hours without updates, tempers rose, and the pilot said fuel could not be bought by card because Myanmar is under sanctions, so the Bangladesh mission brought cash. The trip took 12 hours.

facts.statement: On 1 January (English New Year's Day; the article is published 10 February 2026), a Biman Bangladesh Kuala Lumpur-Dhaka flight departing at 6:45 am (numbered BG 286 in the text, BG 387 in the headline), carrying mostly Bangladeshi migrant workers going home, could not land at Dhaka, Chattogram or Sylhet because of fog and diverted to Yangon, Myanmar, after about three hours of flying; the normal KL-Dhaka flight time is 3 hours 40 minutes.

On the diverted Biman flight, passengers were kept about three hours in the plane at Yangon with weak air-conditioning, little food and no updates from crew or pilot until passengers went to the pilot; the pilot then said fuel could not be bought by debit/credit card because Myanmar is under sanctions, so the Bangladesh mission was bringing cash to buy fuel. Passengers were then given pink dummy tickets and allowed to rest at gate 11 of Yangon airport for about an hour; the whole trip to Dhaka took 12 hours.

Many of the migrant workers on the flight had travelled overnight by bus from far away to reach Kuala Lumpur airport on very short leave; during the delay one worker filmed a vlog walking through the plane urging other workers not to send remittances in protest at their suffering.
The writer describes the Bangladeshi workers from Malaysia on the flight as living in inhuman conditions and doing 16-hour duties.
Prothom Alo's 'Nagorik Songbad' reader section takes stories at email ns@prothomalo.com.

headline_en: Those going abroad rely on the 'minus' market
summary_en: People leaving Bangladesh for cold countries such as Russia, Germany, Finland, Italy, Canada, the US and Romania buy cold-weather 'minus products' in Dhaka, mainly on the fifth floor of Anexco Tower next to Bangabazar (40-42 shops), and also at New Market, Nurjahan Market, Uttara-Baridhara outlets and Rafah Fashion on Green Road, Farmgate. The article gives prices for jackets, thermals, shoes, gloves and other items. A Finland-based worker says the gear suits indoor use but outdoor gear must be bought abroad.

facts.statement: Shubhash Chandra (28) of Araihazar, Narayanganj, enrolled in a master's programme at a university in Russia and flew on 22 January 2026; his uncle in Saratov told him to prepare for daytime temperatures of minus 2-3°C and night temperatures of minus 13-14°C, so he bought a 'minus' jacket, gloves, shoes and trousers in Dhaka before leaving.

In Dhaka, cold-weather clothing for people going to cold countries ('minus products') is sold year-round on the fifth floor of Anexco Tower next to Bangabazar, in 40-42 shops (moved there after the Bangabazar fire), and also at New Market, Nurjahan Market, outlets in Uttara-Baridhara, and Rafah Fashion on Green Road, Farmgate, which sells full sets and can make sets to suit the destination's temperature.

Prices at Dhaka's 'minus' market (Anexco Tower) in early 2026: jackets 2,000-12,000 taka depending on quality; thermal inner 500-1,000 taka; waterproof trousers 1,000-1,200 taka; sherpa hoodie 1,000-1,300 taka; shoes 2,000-4,000 taka; socks 150 taka; waterproof gloves 400-700 taka; cap 400 taka.

A seller at KS Winter Fashion, Anexco Tower, said a North Face jacket costs 70,000-80,000 taka abroad, while a similar jacket sells for 5,000-6,000 taka at his shop; goods come from buying houses and Chattogram factories, including cancelled-shipment stock and fresh orders.
facts.source_in_article: Md Redwan (30), seller at KS Winter Fashion; Aminul Islam, Ashraf Garments

facts.statement: A Bangladeshi working in Finland said the clothing from Dhaka's 'minus' market is fine for wearing at home but not much use outdoors; outdoor gear has to be bought after arriving there.
facts.source_in_article: Mahmudul Hasan (37), works in Finland, travelling back in February 2026

headline_en: Rangpur division: no one keeps promises, the interim government didn't either
summary_en: An opinion column on Rangpur division's neglect in development spending. It says about 250 recruiting agencies got new licences in the past 16 months but Rangpur division got not even four or five, for failing conditions. It also reports that the Expatriates' Welfare Ministry sought 50 acres from BEZA for a 'skills processing zone', and that three Japanese companies were ready, with an MoU, to set up a car-driving training track on 30 acres to take 10,000 drivers a year, but got no land after at least five meetings.

facts.statement: About 250 recruiting agencies received new licences in the 16 months before January 2026; fewer than four or five of them were in Rangpur division, which officials said was because applicants there could not meet the conditions.

Over the six months to January 2026 the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment held several meetings with BEZA (Bangladesh Economic Zones Authority) seeking 50 acres for a 'skills processing zone' where institutions from around the world would invest in nursing training institutes, pre-fab housing, 6G welding and other sectors, with Singapore-standard training centres.

Zia Hasan, economist and policy adviser to the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, wrote on Facebook that three Japanese companies were ready with money, technology and set-up to build a car-driving training track needing 30 acres, would take 10,000 drivers a year, had an MoU ready and could set up within three months of getting land; with 30 acres they would have trained and taken 30,000 workers including language training within 6 months.
facts.source_in_article: Zia Hasan's Facebook post, quoted by columnist

facts.statement: The Japanese investors met Professor Yunus and asked for land and were told to look at Kaliakair; after at least five meetings no positive response was given, according to ministry policy adviser Zia Hasan.
facts.source_in_article: Zia Hasan via columnist Nahid Hasan

headline_en: Russia forcing Bangladeshis into the Ukraine war with job promises
summary_en: An Associated Press investigation, reported by Prothom Alo, found Bangladeshi migrant workers were lured to Russia with false promises of civilian jobs and forced to fight in the Ukraine war. Three who escaped said they were made to sign Russian-language papers that turned out to be military contracts, trained in drone warfare, evacuation and heavy weapons, and forced into front-line tasks under threat of 10 years' prison and beatings. Victims said they saw hundreds of Bangladeshis with Russian forces.

facts.statement: A labour broker persuaded Maksudur Rahman to leave his home town in Bangladesh for Russia with a promise of work as a janitor; within a few weeks of reaching Moscow he was on the front line of the Ukraine war.

Three Bangladeshis who escaped the Russian army told AP that on arrival in Russia they were forced to sign papers written in Russian that turned out to be military contracts, then taken to an army training camp for basic training in drone warfare, evacuating wounded and heavy weapons.
When Maksudur Rahman protested, a Russian commander told him through a translation app: 'Your agent sent you here. We bought you.'

The three escaped Bangladeshis said they were forced against their will into very dangerous front-line work: advancing ahead of Russian troops, carrying supplies, evacuating wounded soldiers and recovering bodies of the dead. Families of three more missing Bangladeshis said their relatives described similar experiences before going missing.
Bangladeshis forced to fight for Russia were threatened with 10 years' imprisonment and beaten if they refused to work; Maksudur Rahman escaped and returned home after seven months.

It is not clear how many Bangladeshis have been tricked this way, but victims told AP they saw hundreds of Bangladeshis with Russian forces in Ukraine. Russia's defence and foreign ministries and the Bangladesh government did not answer AP's questions.

AP reviewed travel papers, Russian military contracts, medical and police reports and photos of war injuries as evidence of the Bangladeshis' participation in the Ukraine war; officials and rights activists say Russia has used the same tactic on citizens of India, Nepal and other South Asian and African countries.

headline_en: Who will be hit by this Trump decision
summary_en: The US is suspending immigrant-visa processing for citizens of 75 countries including Bangladesh from 21 January 2026, for people seeking to live permanently in the US; tourist, business, temporary and other non-immigrant visas are not affected. Applicants can still apply but no immigrant visa will be approved or issued during the suspension, which has no set end date; dual nationals applying on a passport of an unlisted country are exempt. The article also lists other Trump restrictions, including the USD 100,000 H-1B fee.

facts.statement: From 21 January 2026 the United States suspends immigrant-visa processing for citizens of 75 countries including Bangladesh; it applies only to people who want to live permanently in the US, and tourists and short-term visa holders are not covered.
facts.source_in_article: US State Department, via Prothom Alo

facts.statement: During the US immigrant-visa suspension (from 21 January 2026), citizens of the listed countries including Bangladesh can still submit immigrant-visa applications, but no immigrant visa will be approved or issued; the US has given no date for lifting it.
A dual national who applies for a US immigrant visa using a valid passport of a country not on the suspension list is exempt from the January 2026 suspension.
The January 2026 US immigrant-visa suspension does not apply to non-immigrant, temporary, tourist or business visas.

The US State Department told consulates to stop processing immigrant visas for the 75 listed countries, following a November 2025 order to tighten screening of prospective immigrants who could become a financial burden; during the pause it will re-evaluate procedures so that foreigners who might take public welfare funds and benefits cannot enter.

Other South Asian countries on the January 2026 US immigrant-visa suspension list with Bangladesh are Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bhutan and Nepal; the 75-country list also includes Myanmar, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Thailand, Cambodia, Russia, Egypt, Libya, Morocco, Brazil, Colombia and others.
facts.source_in_article: US State Department list via Prothom Alo

facts.statement: In September 2025 the US raised the H-1B visa application fee, used by US companies to hire foreign workers, to USD 100,000 at once.

US restrictions in 2025: a full travel ban on 12 countries in June 2025 (Afghanistan, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea, Eritrea, Haiti, Iran, Libya, Myanmar, Somalia, Sudan, Yemen), extended after November 2025 to six more (Palestine, Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, South Sudan, Syria); a FY2026 refugee cap of 7,500; and a pause on asylum applications and on citizenship and green-card processing for citizens of the first-banned countries.

headline_en: Four including suspected human trafficker arrested at Chapainawabganj border
summary_en: BGB arrested three Bangladeshis trying to cross illegally into India at Bokchar border, Chapainawabganj Sadar, on Wednesday evening 14 January 2026, along with an alleged trafficker, Md Shahin, who was helping them. They told BGB they planned to go to Chennai, India, to work as masons. All four were handed to police and a case was filed.

facts.statement: At about 7 pm on Wednesday 14 January 2026, BGB arrested three Bangladeshis in a village 200 yards inside the zero line at Bokchar border, Chapainawabganj Sadar upazila, as they tried to cross illegally into India; they said they planned, with alleged trafficker Md Shahin's help, to go to Chennai, India, to work as masons (rajmistri).
facts.source_in_article: Lt Col Kazi Mustafizur Rahman, commander of BGB 53 Battalion

facts.statement: The four arrested at Bokchar border on 14 January 2026 (Mizanur Rahman of Chandpur-Lohlamari, Shibganj; Shafiqul Islam of Assam Colony, Rajshahi city; Tarajul Islam of Durgapur, Mithapukur, Rangpur; and alleged trafficker Md Shahin, son of Ebadul Islam of Bokchar, Chapainawabganj Sadar) were handed to Chapainawabganj Sadar police and a case was filed against them.
facts.source_in_article: BGB; Sadar police OC Nure Alam
